title: Laboratory Quality Management System
shortDescription: The document hierarchy and operational backbone every accredited lab runs on — from quality policy down to the individual record.
genZNote: Every accreditation standard eventually asks the same question: show me the system, not just the result.

sections.heading: What a Laboratory QMS Actually Is
sections.body: A Quality Management System (QMS) is the coordinated set of policies, processes, procedures, and records a laboratory uses to consistently meet quality requirements and improve over time. Accreditation doesn't just check whether today's result was correct — it checks whether the SYSTEM that produced it is reliable enough to keep producing correct results.

sections.heading: The Document Hierarchy
sections.body: Every accredited lab's documentation follows roughly the same top-down structure — broader intent at the top, specific evidence at the bottom.
bullets: Quality policy — the lab's top-level commitment to quality, set by management.
Quality objectives — specific, measurable targets that operationalise the policy.
Quality manual (where applicable) — describes the QMS itself and how it meets the standard's requirements.
SOPs (Standard Operating Procedures) — step-by-step instructions for how a specific activity is done.
Work instructions — finer-grained detail for a specific task or piece of equipment, where an SOP alone isn't enough.
Forms — blank templates used to capture data as work is performed.
Records — forms once filled in; the actual evidence that the work happened, and how.

sections.heading: Keeping the System Under Control
bullets: Document control and version control — only the current, approved version of any document should ever be in use.
Record control — records must be legible, retrievable, protected, and retained for a defined period.
Personnel competency — tracked and re-verified, not assumed to be permanent.
Equipment calibration and maintenance — scheduled, documented, and traceable.
Reagent control — storage conditions, lot tracking, expiry management.
Environmental conditions — monitored where they affect result validity (temperature, humidity, contamination control).
Internal audits and management review — the lab checking itself, and leadership formally reviewing whether the whole system is working.
Corrective action and continual improvement — closing the loop when something goes wrong, and improving even when nothing has.

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: A laboratory Quality Management System is the coordinated hierarchy of policy, procedures, and records that lets a lab consistently meet quality requirements — accreditation assesses the system, not just individual results.
keyFacts: Document hierarchy runs: Quality policy → Objectives → (Quality manual) → SOPs → Work instructions → Forms → Records.
A form is blank; a record is that same form filled in — evidence the work actually happened.
Document control ensures only the current approved version of any procedure is in use.
Management review and internal audit are both required, ongoing system checks — not one-time steps.
commonConfusion: A form and a record are often used loosely as the same word — a form is the blank template; a record is that form once filled in, and it's the record (not the blank form) that serves as evidence during an assessment.

highYieldFacts: The document hierarchy always narrows from broad intent (policy) to specific evidence (records).
SOPs describe HOW an activity is done; work instructions add finer task-level detail where needed.
Management review and internal audits are distinct: internal audit checks conformance; management review evaluates the system's overall effectiveness and direction.
commonTraps: Treating 'document' and 'record' as interchangeable — they occupy different, specific positions in the hierarchy (covered fully in the Documentation & Quality Records chapter).
mustRemember: Quality Policy → Objectives → SOPs → Work Instructions → Forms → Records — know this order.

confusedTerms.distinction: An SOP is a step-by-step procedure for an activity; a work instruction gives finer-grained, often equipment- or task-specific detail beyond what the SOP covers.

possibleQuestions: Draw and explain the laboratory quality-system document hierarchy from policy to record.

sources.name: NABL — National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories

pathways.title: The Quality System Document Hierarchy
steps: Quality policy — the lab's top-level commitment
Procedures / SOPs — how each activity is done
Forms — blank templates to capture data
Records — completed forms; the actual evidence

questions.prompt: Which comes immediately after 'Quality objectives' in the standard document hierarchy?
questions.explanation: The hierarchy runs Policy → Objectives → SOPs → Work instructions → Forms → Records.

questions.prompt: What is the key difference between a 'form' and a 'record'?
options: A form is blank; a record is a form that has been filled in
A record is blank; a form is a completed record
Forms are electronic, records are paper
questions.explanation: A form is the template; once filled in during actual work, it becomes a record — the evidence.
